problem: Learned navigation policies typically take raw or mid-level visual inputs such as RGB, depth or 2D segmentation. They must then learn latent 3D geometry, topology and semantics, and learn memory implicitly through RNNs. Prior graph-based navigation work instead predicts only subgoals over flat, offline-built graphs, relies on an external low-level controller, needs prior knowledge of the environment, or is task-specific.
motivation: Modern spatial perception systems (Kimera, 3D Dynamic Scene Graphs) can already build hierarchical metric-semantic maps (objects, places, rooms) online. Feeding these high-level abstractions and explicit trajectory memory to a policy should improve sample efficiency and generalization, much as mid-level representations improved on raw pixels. The paper's premise is that scene hierarchy captures task regularities, e.g. targets are more likely in certain room types. What is missing is a way to connect a globally-defined graph to low-level actions.
key_idea: Embed an incrementally accumulated 3D Dynamic Scene Graph into a robot-centric graph observation by attaching an 'Action layer' of free-space nodes around the robot, then train a GCN actor-critic with PPO that reads out from those action nodes to output low-level motion primitives.
insight: The Action layer is what makes graph-to-action learning possible. Removing it collapses performance (Targets Found 8.7% vs 44.2%; collisions 377.9). Connecting action nodes without ESDF free-space/occlusion checks more than doubles collisions (229.8 vs 90.0) and cuts targets to 31.7%. Hierarchy (Room/Object layers) raises targets found (44.2 vs 41.9 Places-only) without extra area explored or fewer collisions, so the gain comes from focusing search on likely rooms. Consistent with this, corrupting semantic labels beyond ~40% drops performance below the No-Hierarchy variant, showing the policy really uses semantics. Explicit memory (DSG accumulation plus a visited flag) mainly prevents revisiting: No Memory explores 53.0 m² vs 59.0 and finds 38.6%.
method: 3D Dynamic Scene Graph input: a hierarchical DSG (Rosinol et al.) with a mesh/ESDF layer, objects, places (topological free-space graph), rooms and building. For training it is built offline per scene and revealed incrementally: Place nodes that are visible (in FOV and not occluded per ESDF), plus their connected Room/Object nodes, are accumulated into the online DSG_t.

Graph observation: all DSG_t nodes and edges except the mesh and building node, with positions transformed into the robot frame. Each node gets a 10-D feature: relative xyz position, bbox dimensions (objects), node category, semantic class, a binary traversed flag (robot passed within d_t=2 m, or action node is free), and the ESDF value.

Action layer: 8 nodes evenly placed on a circle of radius r_a=1 m around the robot. An action node is connected to a DSG node if (1) it lies in free space (ESDF > d_f=0.1 m), (2) the DSG node is within d_a=1 m, and (3) the straight line between them is free (Bresenham raycast on a 2D ESDF slice).
GNN backbone: 3 iterations of 64-channel GCN message passing with ReLU (PyTorch Geometric). Readout is a 2-layer 512-wide MLP over the stacked Action-layer node features only.

Actor-critic policy: a shared GNN backbone feeds 1-layer MLP actor and critic heads. It is trained with RLlib PPO for 10^6 steps (lr 1e-4, batch 4096, minibatch 128, 30 SGD iterations, gamma 0.99, GAE 0.9) and outputs a distribution over {forward 0.5 m, turn left 8°, turn right 8°}.
Memory: explicit memory comes from DSG accumulation over the episode plus the per-node visited flag, rather than an RNN.

setting.backbone: 3-layer 64-channel GCN + MLP readout and actor/critic heads (trained from scratch with PPO)
setting.training_data: RL (PPO, 10^6 steps) in 4 training office environments (3,880 m² total) of a Unity-based simulator; tested on 3 unseen environments (4,850 m²); no external or pretraining data
setting.observation: Graph observation derived from an incrementally revealed 3D Dynamic Scene Graph (places, objects, rooms, with semantics) plus ESDF. The DSG is built from ground-truth RGB, semantic segmentation, depth and inertial data.
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: move forward 0.5 m / turn left 8° / turn right 8°
setting.privileged: DSG pre-built offline from ground-truth simulator data (GT semantics, depth, localization) and revealed by a visibility check; GT ESDF used for free-space/occlusion checks. Baselines receive GT pose.

numbers.extra: GT-derived DSG revealed incrementally; 30 targets, 400-step budget, 2 m collection radius; test on unseen Environments 5-7

numbers_note: Custom task and environment with no standard navigation benchmark; metrics are % targets found, number of collisions, and area explored (m²), with 95% bootstrap CIs. Other own variants not listed: No Occ. Check is 31.7/229.8/35.7 (Table 3); Delayed Rooms is 43.0/98.0/57.7 (Table A3). Robustness to position and semantic noise is reported only in appendix figures (e.g. text: 'collects 40% of the targets with SD = 0.5 m'). Table 3 prints the Proposed CI as (42.7, 45.2) vs (42.7, 45.7) elsewhere.
results: On unseen office environments the DSG-GNN policy finds 44.2% of targets and explores 59.1 m². The strongest visuomotor baseline, RGB-D + Sem. (PPO+GRU with GT pose), reaches 39.7% and 53.3 m²; RGB gets 38.4% and ESDF-slice 31.6%. The proposed policy collides more than RGB-D + Sem. (90.0 vs 45.3), which the authors attribute to the sparse Places layer being a poor source of free-space information. Ablations confirm the Action layer, occlusion checking, hierarchy and explicit memory each contribute.
limitations: Obstacle avoidance from sparse graph data is weaker: roughly 2x more collisions than the RGB-D + Sem. baseline.
Simulation only, in a single custom Unity office task. The DSG is pre-built offline from ground-truth data rather than constructed online by real perception (Hydra integration left to future work).
Sensitive to node position noise: targets found falls from 44.2% to ~31.7% at 1 m SD and ~15.6% at 2 m SD. Training is 5.5x slower than the RGB baseline.
